extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, reviewers, researchers studying peer review, and academic policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and recommended practices for evaluating and improving the academic journal peer-review process, including ethical requirements, reviewer selection and calibration, editorial responsibilities, and experimental designs to study review bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the Matthew Effect in bias analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that eminent authors/institutions may receive easier publication and more favorable reception (the 'Matthew Effect') and consider whether this helps or hinders scientific development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether prestigious authors' work is being favored beyond its intrinsic merit and investigate the functional significance (helpful vs. dysfunctional) for the discipline. Consider that halo effects may help some authors and hurt others but may not change overall literature quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of 'importance' of articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether a manuscript is 'important' — i.e., likely to have major implications for a subspecialty or be perceived as controversial — because importance affects familiarity and reviewer detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use citation history cautiously (one or two citations does not imply major importance). Recognize many submissions are 'minor' and decisions may hinge on halo characteristics for such pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise / subspecialty familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Select reviewers likely familiar with the specific subspecialty so they can properly recognize and evaluate manuscripts, since only a handful of practitioners read any given article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning reviewers outside the manuscript's narrow specialty. Acknowledge that with many journals and thousands of articles, reviewer unfamiliarity is a frequent cause of failures to detect issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent from original authors for research using their work
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain informed consent from authors if their previously published articles are to be used in research that resubmits or otherwise manipulates their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to secure consent risks embarrassment and ethical violations; such consent is considered essential when human subjects (here, authors) may be harmed by the research design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright/permission compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain permission from publishers before reproducing articles for research use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to secure publisher permission may violate copyright law; researchers must check and comply with copyright requirements before reproducing or resubmitting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deception of editors and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not deceive editors, associate editors, or referees as unwitting participants in experiments without ethical approval and justifiable cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive procedures that misuse voluntary professional activity are ethically questionable; alternatives (e.g., honest randomized editorial studies) should be pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality of review materials and reviewer-author communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect implicit understandings that reviewers' comments/recommendations are available to editors and authors only under agreed conditions; do not disclose review content inappropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not provide reviewers' private materials to third parties without consent; be cautious about quoted criticisms that might identify original authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid identifiable quotations that reveal original authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that reporting or quoting reviewer comments does not make original authors identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing or discussing reviews, redact or generalize sufficiently to prevent identification, especially in cases where authors could be singled out by distinctive quoted critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design studies of peer review with proper methodological controls
rubrics_metrics.description: When experimentally studying peer review, explicitly control and stratify for author status, reviewer status, and blind vs nonblind review to measure main effects and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use randomized assignment within strata (e.g., Latin square designs) and analyze main and interaction effects. Track reviewer identities to avoid confounding reviewer change with other manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track reviewer identity in resubmission studies to avoid confounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether the reviewers on resubmission are the same as on the original submission because change in reviewers can confound effects attributed to other manipulations (e.g., authorship changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without reviewer-level data you cannot estimate how much of an observed effect is due to different reviewers rather than the experimental variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for reviewer seniority and cohort effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that younger reviewers may be systematically tougher than senior reviewers; reviewer age/cohort can bias acceptance probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance reviewer seniority across conditions or control for it analytically when interpreting findings about bias or acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include controls for both positive and negative status biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Test and control for both kinds of status bias: positive bias favoring prestigious institutions/authors and negative bias against unusual or low-prestige-sounding institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include neutral or credible-but-less-prestigious institutional names as controls to detect whether effects are positive favoritism or negative prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use behaviorally anchored criteria and reviewer training
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop clear, behaviorally anchored evaluation criteria for reviewers and train them until interjudge reliability reaches acceptable levels before relying on their judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conducting an experiment or relying on reviewer judgments for important decisions, calibrate reviewers to those criteria and withhold use of judgments until reliability is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should monitor and calibrate reviewer strictness
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must evaluate referees' performance, adjust for systematic strictness or leniency among reviewers, and make final decisions that account for these differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a simple tally of referee votes; editors should normalize for reviewer harshness and exercise judgment rather than acting as clerks who merely tabulate recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow authors a chance to counterargue referees' criticisms before final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Send referees' comments to authors for their counterarguments and consider authors' responses before making a final accept/reject decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing authors an opportunity to reply can reduce the weight of a single poor or incorrect referee report and improve decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must act as true decision-makers, not clerks
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should read manuscripts and reviews carefully, resolve conflicting recommendations, and exercise independent judgment rather than relying solely on reviewer votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires sufficient editorial time and commitment; journals with high submission loads should employ additional editors to preserve decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manageable editorial workload standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of submissions handled by a single editor to a level that permits thoughtful decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested upper bound: 150–175 submissions per year per editor; journals exceeding that should have multiple editors to distribute workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and transparency in rejection letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft rejection letters that acknowledge the provisional nature of the evaluation, summarize points of agreement and disagreement with referees, and avoid dogmatic or condescending language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enclosed referee comments, state where you agree and disagree with them, and explain that the decision reflects scarce journal space rather than definitive evaluation. Example template provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate weighting of referee reports (avoid overreliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rigidly make decisions solely based on referee reports; recognize that referee reports can be inconsistent or incorrect and should not be given disproportionate weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider systems that reduce the impact of a single bad report without undermining the value of peer review; avoid changes that either place too much or too little weight on referees' recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with reforms that merely change peripheral features
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that peripheral reforms (e.g., double-blind review, automatic abstract publication) may not eliminate poor or incorrect referee reports by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target reforms to reduce the incidence and consequences of poor reviews (editorial oversight, reviewer training, author rebuttals) rather than relying solely on procedural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical requirement: minimize harm and respect professional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Design studies and editorial practices that preserve trust, confidentiality, and the voluntary nature of peer-review participation; avoid practices that abuse the professional contribution of reviewers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional review boards and editors should work to ensure research on peer review is conducted with integrity; where deception is proposed, consider whether the results could be obtained without it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use randomized experimental designs within editorial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors interested in studying peer-review effects can implement randomized designs on live submissions (e.g., stratify by author status and randomize reviewer pairings) to measure status, reviewer, and blinding effects ethically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs such as Latin squares and stratified randomization permit estimation of main effects and interactions without deceptive practices toward reviewers; analyze data with appropriate factorial methods.
